name: Catalan (Balearic)
variety: Balearic Catalan (Eastern dialect group), described from Majorcan; Minorcan and Ibizan differ mainly in the treatment of unstressed o
sources: Carbonell, Joan F. and Llisterri, Joaquim (1992). Catalan. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 22(1-2), 53-56. Reprinted in the Handbook of the International Phonetic Association (1999), Cambridge University Press.
Wheeler, Max W. (2005). The Phonology of Catalan. Oxford University Press.
Recasens, Daniel (1996). Fonètica descriptiva del català. 2nd edition. Barcelona: Institut d'Estudis Catalans.
Veny, Joan (1982). Els parlars catalans: síntesi de dialectologia. Palma: Moll.
Bibiloni, Gabriel (2016). El català de Mallorca: la fonètica. Palma: Lleonard Muntaner.

Recasens, Daniel and Espinosa, Aina (2005). Articulatory, positional and coarticulatory characteristics for clear /l/ and dark /l/: evidence from two Catalan dialects. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 35(1), 1-25.
Recasens, Daniel and Espinosa, Aina (2006). Dispersion and variability of Catalan vowels. Speech Communication 48, 645-666.

Recasens, Daniel and Espinosa, Aina (2007). An electropalatographic and acoustic study of affricates and fricatives in two Catalan dialects. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 37(2), 143-172.
Institut d'Estudis Catalans (2016). Gramàtica de la llengua catalana. Barcelona: IEC.
Prieto, Pilar et al. (2015). Intonational phonology of Catalan and its dialectal varieties. In Frota and Prieto (eds.), Intonation in Romance. Oxford University Press.
contrasts: eight vowels under stress: /i e ɛ a ɔ o u/ plus stressed /ə/, which continues the close e of early Romance (set [sət] 'thirst' versus set [sɛt] 'seven'; pera [ˈpəɾə], ceba [ˈsəβə], cadena [kəˈðənə])
four vowels in unstressed syllables in most of Majorca [i ə o u]; three [i ə u] in Minorca, Ibiza and the Sóller area
/v/ is kept distinct from /b/ (vi [vi] versus bé [be])
/s/ versus /z/, /ʃ/ versus /ʒ/, affricates /tʃ dʒ ts dz/
obstruent voicing is neutralised at the end of a word
allophony: unstressed /a ɛ e/ are [ə]; unstressed /o ɔ/ stay [o] in most of Majorca, but become [u] before a stressed high vowel (cosí [kuˈzi], comú [kuˈmu]) and everywhere in Minorca and Ibiza
/k ɡ/ are palatal stops [c ɟ] before front vowels and at the end of a word in much of Majorca (Palma, Manacor), in some towns also before /a/

the old palatal lateral from Latin LY, C'L, G'L is [j] (ull [uj], fill [fij], palla [ˈpajə], vell [vej]) and may be lost next to a front vowel; the lateral from Latin LL and from initial L stays [ʎ] (cavall [kəˈvaʎ], ella, aquell, llop)
/l/ is strongly velarised [ɫ] in all positions, more than in the other dialects (Recasens and Espinosa 2005)
final clusters keep their stop: pont [pɔnt], camp [kamp], alt [alt], molt [molt]; the first person singular of the present has no ending (jo cant)
word-final r is silent in most words, as in Central Catalan
strong regressive assimilation in consonant clusters, within words and across them: dissabte [diˈsattə], cap moix [kam ˈmoʃ], amics [əˈmits]
/b d ɡ/ are approximants [β ð ɣ] after vowels and continuants
word-final obstruents are voiceless before pause and take the voicing of a following consonant; final sibilants are voiced before a vowel
nouns in unstressed -ia lose the final vowel in everyday speech: història [isˈtɔɾi], família [fəˈmili]
nasals assimilate in place to the following consonant
phonotactics: word-final clusters of sonorant plus stop are pronounced in full
stop plus consonant sequences become geminates or assimilated clusters
/ɾ/ does not begin a word; /ʎ/ and /ɲ/ occur in all positions
the definite article is es, sa (from Latin ipse) in everyday speech

stress.type: lexical, on one of the last three syllables
stress.rule: Words ending in a vowel, a vowel plus s, or -en, -in are stressed on the penultimate syllable, other words on the last; all exceptions carry a written accent.
stress.cues: vowel quality, duration and pitch; stressed [ə] shows that schwa quality alone does not signal lack of stress

rhythm.vowel_reduction: strong in quality for a and e, which become [ə]; o is kept in most of Majorca; reduced vowels are not deleted, apart from final -a after i
rhythm.notes: No rhythm measurements specific to Balearic are cited here.

length.notes: Geminates are frequent because stop plus consonant clusters assimilate (dissabte [diˈsattə], setmana [səmˈmanə]); they are not contrastive in the lexicon in the way Italian geminates are.

intonation.declarative: rising accents with a delayed peak before the nucleus, low nuclear accent on the last stressed syllable and low boundary
intonation.yes_no_question: mostly falling: a high stretch up to the last stressed syllable, a fall on that syllable and a low boundary (¡H+L* L%), with or without an opening particle (que, o)
intonation.wh_question: high on the question word, falling to a low boundary
intonation.continuation: rising accent with high boundary at the end of non-final phrases
intonation.accent_shape: prenuclear L+<H* with the peak after the stressed syllable; nuclear L* in statements, H+L* in questions
intonation.notes: Prieto et al. (2015) describe falling yes-no questions as the normal Balearic pattern, against the rising pattern that is common in Central, North-western and Valencian Catalan.

problems: the change of ʎ to [j] is applied to every ʎ after a vowel, also to the lateral from Latin LL, which Majorcan keeps: cavall is [kəvˈaj], aquell [əkˈəj], allà [əjˈa], bella [bˈejə], ella [ˈeə]
no palatal stops [c ɟ]: qui, guerra, sac, amic have velar [k ɡ]

stressed [ə] depends on a word list and spelling rules and misses common words (ceba, cera, negre keep [ɛ]), while every written 'è' becomes [ə], also in learned and borrowed words where Majorcan has [ɛ] (cafè [kəfˈə], ciència [siˈənsiə], València [vəlˈənsiə])
unstressed o is never raised before a stressed high vowel (conill [konˈij], cosí [kozˈi], comú [komˈu]), and there is no setting for the Minorcan and Ibizan reduction of every unstressed o to [u]
/l/ imports the English phoneme, dark only in the coda, although Majorcan has the darkest l of all Catalan dialects in all positions
no tune set is selected, so the generic default tunes are used; the falling yes-no question is not modelled
good: /v/ is kept apart from /b/, and unstressed o is not reduced to [u]
final clusters keep their stop (pont [pˈɔnt], camp [kˈamp], alt [ˈalt]) and final r is silent
cluster assimilation follows the description in the grammar of the Institut d'Estudis Catalans (amics [əmˈits], dissabte [disˈattə], cap moix [kˈam mˈoʃ])
home is given its Majorcan form [ˈɔmo]

notes: The voice combines rule sets 1 and 4 of ca_rules with its own phoneme table. It models Majorcan; Minorcan and Ibizan speakers differ in unstressed o and in several consonant details.
